chapter: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
title: Water boy on the Pacific Electric line
summary: He carried water to track-laying crews building the red car line to Long Beach for a dollar a day.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: So after the tailor business, where did you work?

Well, after that, I don't know. I went in the post office, but before I went in the post office, I worked on the railroad. When they built the big old red cars--you don't remember them--when they had the big old red cars that'd run to the beaches and all.

Well, when they first built, they built from Ninth and Main Street down Ninth Street to Alame...to Long Beach [Boulevard] and all the way to Long Beach [city of Long Beach]. Well, I worked on that from Ninth and Main to Long Beach. I got a dollar a day and a dollar-and-a-half a night, two dollars for Sunday, as a water boy.
Well, you know, they had forty to a hundred
to a hundred and fifty men [laying] those rails and digging them, and you carry the water for them to drink.
Oh, I see, they were building the line. Oh.

Yeah. There was five or six of us water boys, and the Mexicans yell, "Agua! Agua!" That means he wants some water, and you carry it. They drink every bit of it 'cause they're lazy rascals, and every time you...your bucket get empty, you got to go get some water. Sometime you got to walk a half-mile to get the water almost because it was like, between here and Long Beach, there wasn't no houses out there near the tracks or anything. Sometime you'd have to walk from here to Western Avenue almost to find water, you know. Then they got so they used to take barrels of water on the flat cars. You know, and we'd get water that way.
What year was that they built that line? Do you remember?
